idiom_name: x => x — the arrow identity as neutral element of compose/reduce
implementation_notes: ECMAScript has no built-in identity function, but first-class functions plus the ES2015 arrow expression make the pattern a one-liner: const identity = x => x (no wrapper class, interface, or strategy object is needed — the classic structure collapses entirely into a first-class function value). The composition neutral element lives in the initialValue slot of Array.prototype.reduce/reduceRight: compose = (...fns) => x => fns.reduceRight((acc, f) => f(acc), x) reduces an empty function list to identity and avoids the TypeError that reduce throws on an empty array without an initial value; in FP codebases the canonical names are Ramda's R.identity and Lodash's _.identity (which is also the documented default predicate/iteratee of _.map, _.filter, _.find, _.uniqBy and friends). The hand-rolled arrow stays justified whenever a shared canonical import would be the only reason to pull in a utility library; hoist it once at module level rather than re-creating it per call site. V8 and other JIT engines inline tiny arrows in hot paths, so a hoisted identity is effectively free, while a freshly allocated arrow per call still costs an allocation.
pitfalls: Identity as a default predicate coerces through JS truthiness: R.filter(R.identity, xs) and _.filter(xs) drop every falsy element — 0, '', false, NaN included — not just null/undefined; when only absence should be filtered, write an explicit predicate such as x => x != null (or R.reject(R.isNil)) instead of leaning on identity truthiness.

Array.prototype.reduce calls back with four arguments (accumulator, value, index, array); a composition helper that leaks the extra arguments into step functions with optional parameters silently misbehaves — the same dynamic-typing trap as ['1','2','3'].map(parseInt) yielding [1, NaN, NaN] — because no compiler catches the arity mismatch.

The identity arrow returns the same reference, not a copy: callers that mutate the value they received 'unchanged' mutate the original object, which surprises code that treats pass-through as isolation; freeze or clone explicitly when downstream mutation is possible.

Calling xs.reduce(step) without an initial value throws a TypeError on an empty array — pipelines that seed composition with identity avoid the crash and keep the empty-pipeline case well-defined (an empty function list reduces to identity itself).

Allocating a fresh arrow identity inside a factory or render function adds a function object per call and breaks memoization-by-reference downstream; hoist a single module-level const identity = x => x.

Never use identity as a promise rejection handler: .catch(identity) resolves with the rejection reason instead of rethrowing, silently turning failures into successful values — rethrow with e => { throw e; } or omit the handler entirely.
